reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by mutations in the BTK gene, which encodes Bruton tyrosine kinase, a signalling molecule essential for B-cell maturation
The block in B-cell development leads to near-absent circulating B cells and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes
Affected boys typically become symptomatic after about 6 months of age as maternally transferred IgG wanes

Recurrent infections are dominated by encapsulated pyogenic bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, causing sinopulmonary infections, otitis, and sometimes sepsis or meningitis
Patients are particularly vulnerable to enteroviruses, which can cause chronic meningoencephalitis, and historically to vaccine-associated poliovirus
Physical examination often reveals scanty tonsils and lymphoid tissue because germinal centres do not form
Cellular (T-cell) immunity is intact, so most viral and fungal infections are handled normally, distinguishing it from combined immunodeficiencies
The cornerstone of treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement together with prompt antibiotic treatment of infections
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from loss-of-function mutations in BTK, a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that transmits signals from the pre-B-cell and B-cell receptors. Without functional BTK, developing B cells arrest at the pre-B stage in the bone marrow and fail to mature, so mature B cells and plasma cells are largely absent from the periphery and lymphoid tissue. The consequence is a profound deficiency of all antibody classes, leaving the patient unable to opsonise and clear encapsulated bacteria and unable to neutralise certain viruses, notably enteroviruses. Because T-cell and innate immunity are preserved, the clinical picture is dominated by pyogenic bacterial and enteroviral infection rather than opportunistic disease.
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulin levels (markedly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM)
Lymphocyte subsets showing very low or absent CD19/CD20 B cells with normal T cells
BTK gene sequencing and BTK protein expression analysis
Specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide antigens (poor or absent)
Imaging of chest and sinuses to assess for bronchiectasis and chronic infection
Enteroviral testing (including cerebrospinal fluid) when chronic neurological symptoms occur
redFlags: Recurrent or severe sinopulmonary infection or sepsis warranting urgent immunological assessment
Chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis presenting with progressive neurological decline
Live vaccines, especially oral polio, must be avoided because of the antibody defect
Progressive bronchiectasis from repeated or inadequately treated respiratory infection
Failure to thrive with recurrent infection in an infant boy after 6 months of age
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and consistent immunoglobulin replacement plus prompt antibiotic therapy, most patients have a good long-term outlook, though chronic lung disease from recurrent respiratory infection and rare enteroviral central nervous system infection remain important causes of morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent childhood infections to ordinary illness and delaying immunoglobulin measurement
Overlooking the physical clue of absent tonsils and lymph nodes
Giving live vaccines, particularly oral poliovirus vaccine
Assuming normal viral immunity fully protects, thereby missing enteroviral complications
Under-dosing or interrupting immunoglobulin replacement, allowing breakthrough infection and lung damage
